parrafos: The euro (symbol: €; currency code: EUR) is the official currency of 21 of the 27 member states of the European Union. This group of states is officially known as the euro area, more commonly named the eurozone. Each euro is subdivided into 100 cents.

The currency is also used officially by the institutions of the European Union, by four European microstates that are not EU members, by one British Overseas Territory, as well as unilaterally by two European states that are not EU members. Outside Europe, a number of special territories of EU members also use the euro as their currency.

The euro is used by 358 million people in the eurozone, in addition to those living in states and territories where the euro is also the sole official currency. Furthermore, over 200 million people worldwide use currencies pegged to the euro. It is the second-largest reserve currency as well as the second-most traded currency in the world after the United States dollar. As of December 2019, with more than €1.3 trillion in circulation, the euro has one of the highest combined values of banknotes and coins in circulation in the world.

The name euro was officially adopted on 16 December 1995 in Madrid. The euro was introduced to world financial markets as an accounting currency on 1 January 1999, replacing the former European Currency Unit (ECU) at a ratio of 1:1. Physical euro coins and banknotes entered into circulation on 1 January 2002, making it the day-to-day operating currency of its original members, and by March 2002 it had completely replaced the former currencies.

Before December 2002, the euro traded below parity with the US dollar; since then, it has traded near or above parity. On 13 July 2022, the two currencies briefly hit parity for the first time in nearly two decades, due in part to the Russian invasion of Ukraine. In the ten years ending 30 September 2025, the rate has averaged at about $1.00:€0.89.

The euro is managed and administered by the European Central Bank and the Eurosystem, composed of the central banks of the eurozone countries. As an independent central bank, the ECB has sole authority to set monetary policy. The Eurosystem participates in the printing, minting and distribution of euro banknotes and coins in all member states, and the operation of the eurozone payment systems.

Through their ratification of the 1992 Maastricht Treaty (or subsequent treaties of accession), most EU member states committed to adopt the euro upon meeting certain monetary and budgetary convergence criteria, although not all participating states have done so. Denmark has negotiated exemptions, while Sweden (which joined the EU in 1995, after the Maastricht Treaty was signed) turned down the euro in a 2003 non-binding referendum, and has circumvented its commitment to adopt the euro by staying out of ERM II. All nations that have joined the EU since 1993 have pledged to adopt the euro in due course. The Maastricht Treaty was amended by the 2001 Treaty of Nice, which closed the gaps and loopholes in the Maastricht and Rome Treaties.

The following five EU member states, representing almost 90 million people, committed themselves in their respective Treaty of Accession to adopt the euro. However they do not have a deadline to do so and can delay the process by deliberately not complying with the convergence criteria (such as by not meeting the convergence criteria to join ERM II).
The Maastricht Treaty of 1992 included protocols on Denmark and also the United Kingdom, giving them opt-outs with the right to decide if and when they would adopt the euro.

Denmark: The government of Denmark negotiated an opt-out to retain usage of the Danish krone, but the currency is pegged to the euro via the ERM II, the European Union's exchange rate mechanism. This same rule applies to Greenland and the Faroe Islands, as they are part of the Kingdom of Denmark and use the krone as their official tender.
In addition, prior to its withdrawal from the European Union in 2020, the United Kingdom negotiated an opt-out to retain usage of the pound sterling.

The euro is divided into 100 cents (also referred to as euro cents, especially when distinguishing them from other currencies, and referred to as such on the common side of all cent coins). In Community legislative acts the plural forms of euro and cent are spelled without the s, notwithstanding normal English usage. Otherwise, normal English plurals are used, with many local variations such as centime in France.

All circulating coins have a common side showing the denomination or value and a map in the background. Due to the linguistic plurality in the European Union, the Latin alphabet version of euro is used (as opposed to the less common Greek or Cyrillic) and Arabic numerals (other text is used on national sides in national languages, but other text on the common side is avoided). For the denominations except the 1-, 2- and 5-cent coins, the map only showed the 15 member states of the union as of 2002. Beginning in 2007 or 2008 (depending on the country), the old map was replaced by a map of Europe also showing countries outside the EU. The 1-, 2- and 5-cent coins, however, keep their old design, showing a geographical map of Europe with the EU member states as of 2002, raised somewhat above the rest of the map. All common sides were designed by Luc Luycx. The coins also have a national side showing an image specifically chosen by the country that issued the coin. Euro coins from any member state may be freely used in any nation that has adopted the euro.

The coins are issued in denominations of €2, €1, 50c, 20c, 10c, 5c, 2c, and 1c. To avoid the use of the two smallest coins, some cash transactions are rounded to the nearest five cents in the Netherlands and Ireland (by voluntary agreement) and in Finland and Italy (by law). This practice is discouraged by the commission, as is the practice of certain shops of refusing to accept high-value euro notes.

Commemorative coins with €2 face value have been issued with changes to the design of the national side of the coin. These include both commonly issued coins, such as the €2 commemorative coin for the fiftieth anniversary of the signing of the Treaty of Rome, and nationally issued coins, such as the coin to commemorate the 2004 Summer Olympics issued by Greece. These coins are legal tender throughout the eurozone. Collector coins with various other denominations have been issued as well, but these are not intended for general circulation, and they are legal tender only in the member state that issued them.

The design for the euro banknotes has common designs on both sides. The design was created by the Austrian designer Robert Kalina. Notes are issued in €500, €200, €100, €50, €20, €10, and €5. Each banknote has its own colour and is dedicated to an artistic period of European architecture. The front of the note features windows or gateways while the back has bridges, symbolising links between states in the union and with the future. While the designs are supposed to be devoid of any identifiable characteristics, the initial designs by Kalina were of specific bridges, including the Rialto and the Pont de Neuilly, and were subsequently rendered more generic; the final designs still bear very close similarities to their specific prototypes; thus they are not truly generic. The monuments looked similar enough to different national monuments to please everyone.

The Europa series, or second series, consists of six denominations and no longer includes the €500 with issuance discontinued as of 27 April 2019. However, both the first and the second series of euro banknotes, including the €500, remain legal tender throughout the euro area.

In December 2021, the ECB announced its plans to redesign euro banknotes by 2024. A theme advisory group, made up of one member from each euro area country, was selected to submit theme proposals to the ECB. The proposals will be voted on by the public; a design competition will also be held.

Since 1 January 2002, the national central banks (NCBs) and the ECB have issued euro banknotes on a joint basis. Eurosystem NCBs are required to accept euro banknotes put into circulation by other Eurosystem members and these banknotes are not repatriated. The ECB issues 8% of the total value of banknotes issued by the Eurosystem. In practice, the ECB's banknotes are put into circulation by the NCBs, thereby incurring matching liabilities vis-à-vis the ECB. These liabilities carry interest at the main refinancing rate of the ECB. The other 92% of euro banknotes are issued by the NCBs in proportion to their respective shares of the ECB capital key, calculated using national share of European Union (EU) population and national share of EU GDP, equally weighted.

Capital within the EU may be transferred in any amount from one state to another. All intra-Union transfers in euro are treated as domestic transactions and bear the corresponding domestic transfer costs. This includes all member states of the EU, even those outside the eurozone providing the transactions are carried out in euro. Credit/debit card charging and ATM withdrawals within the eurozone are also treated as domestic transactions; however paper-based payment orders, like cheques, have not been standardised so these are still domestic-based. The ECB has also set up a clearing system, T2 since March 2023, for large euro transactions.

The euro was established by the provisions in the 1992 Maastricht Treaty. To participate in the currency, member states are meant to meet strict criteria, such as a budget deficit of less than 3% of their GDP, a debt ratio of less than 60% of GDP (both of which were ultimately widely flouted after introduction), low inflation, and interest rates close to the EU average. In the Maastricht Treaty, the United Kingdom and Denmark were granted exemptions per their request from moving to the stage of monetary union which resulted in the introduction of the euro (see also United Kingdom and the euro).
resumen_es: Describes the euro: where it is used and its international weight, its introduction, its management by the ECB and the Eurosystem, the commitments and exceptions regarding adoption, the design of coins and banknotes, how it is issued, and the Maastricht criteria.

ideas_clave.idea: The euro is the currency of 21 of the 27 EU countries, which make up the eurozone, and it is also used by EU institutions and by several non-member states and territories.
Used by 358 million people in the eurozone, it ranks second only to the dollar as a reserve and traded currency and has one of the largest values of cash in circulation.
Named in Madrid in 1995, the euro replaced the ECU as an accounting currency in 1999 and became physical cash in 2002, quickly displacing national currencies.
Its exchange rate has generally been close to or above parity with the dollar since late 2002, briefly touching parity in 2022.
The ECB, as an independent authority, sets monetary policy, while the Eurosystem of national central banks handles cash and payment systems.
Under the Maastricht Treaty most member states pledged to join once they meet convergence criteria, but some can postpone membership indefinitely, as Sweden does by staying out of ERM II.
Denmark and the United Kingdom obtained opt-outs; the Danish krone remains pegged to the euro through ERM II, and the UK kept the pound until it left the EU.
The euro is divided into cents, and coins combine a common European side, designed to avoid linguistic issues, with a national side chosen by each issuing country.
There are eight coin denominations, some countries round cash payments to avoid the smallest coins, and commemorative two-euro coins circulate throughout the eurozone.
Banknotes share common designs of windows and bridges inspired by architectural periods; the €500 note is no longer issued but remains valid, and a redesign has been planned.
Banknotes are issued jointly, with the ECB accounting for 8% of their value and national central banks issuing the rest according to the ECB capital key.
Euro transfers within the EU are treated as domestic payments, and the ECB operates a clearing system for large transactions.
Joining requires meeting the Maastricht criteria on deficits, debt, inflation and interest rates, although the fiscal limits were often ignored after the launch of the currency.

resumen_modelo: The text presents the euro, the official currency of 21 of the 27 European Union member states, which together form the eurozone. Besides being used by EU institutions and several non-member territories, it is the world's second most important reserve and traded currency after the US dollar. Adopted in name in 1995, it was introduced as an accounting currency in 1999, replacing the ECU, and as physical cash in 2002, swiftly supplanting national currencies; since then, it has generally traded close to or above parity with the dollar. Monetary policy is the exclusive responsibility of the independent European Central Bank, whereas the Eurosystem, comprising the national central banks, manages cash and payment systems. Under the Maastricht Treaty, most member states undertook to adopt the euro once they fulfilled certain convergence criteria; nevertheless, some can delay accession indefinitely, as Sweden does, while Denmark and the United Kingdom secured formal opt-outs. Regarding cash, coins feature a common European side and a national side, and some countries round cash payments to avoid the smallest denominations. Banknotes, in turn, depict windows and bridges symbolising European integration; the €500 note is no longer issued, although it remains legal tender. Moreover, notes are issued jointly, the ECB accounting for 8% of their value and national central banks for the remainder according to the capital key. Transfers in euro within the EU are treated as domestic. Finally, entry was meant to be governed by the Maastricht criteria on deficits, debt, inflation and interest rates, although the fiscal limits were widely disregarded.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: The euro is the official currency of all 27 EU member states.
preguntas.cita: the official currency of 21 of the 27 member states of the European Union
preguntas.explicacion: Only 21 of the 27 member states use the euro as their official currency. The statement is false.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the euro's position as a reserve currency?
opciones: It is the second-largest, after the US dollar.
It is the largest in the world.
It is the third-largest, after the dollar and the yen.
It is not used as a reserve currency.
respuestas: It is the second-largest, after the US dollar.
preguntas.cita: It is the second-largest reserve currency as well as the second-most traded currency in the world after the United States dollar.
preguntas.explicacion: The text places the euro as the second reserve currency after the dollar. It is not the first, the yen is not mentioned, and it is indeed used as a reserve currency.

preguntas.pregunta: When did euro coins and banknotes enter into circulation?
preguntas.cita: Physical euro coins and banknotes entered into circulation on 1 January 2002
preguntas.explicacion: Cash was introduced on 1 January 2002. In 1999 the euro was born as an accounting currency, in 1995 the name was adopted, and by March 2002 it had completely replaced the national currencies.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: In July 2022 the euro and the dollar reached parity for the first time in almost twenty years.
preguntas.cita: the two currencies briefly hit parity for the first time in nearly two decades
preguntas.explicacion: On 13 July 2022 the two currencies briefly reached parity, something that had not happened for almost two decades. It is true.

preguntas.pregunta: Find a word meaning 'the production of coins'.
preguntas.cita: The Eurosystem participates in the printing, minting and distribution of euro banknotes and coins
preguntas.explicacion: “Minting” is the making of coins; “printing” refers to producing banknotes.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Sweden rejected the euro in a legally binding referendum in 2003.
preguntas.cita: turned down the euro in a 2003 non-binding referendum
preguntas.explicacion: The 2003 Swedish referendum was not binding. That detail makes the statement false.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: How can the five member states committed to adopting the euro postpone doing so?
respuestas: They have no deadline, so they can delay the process by deliberately failing to meet the convergence criteria, for example by not fulfilling the conditions to join ERM II.
preguntas.cita: they do not have a deadline to do so and can delay the process by deliberately not complying with the convergence criteria
preguntas.explicacion: You should point out the absence of a deadline and the deliberate failure to meet the convergence criteria, particularly those for joining ERM II.

preguntas.pregunta: What is the relationship between the Danish krone and the euro?
opciones: The krone is pegged to the euro through ERM II.
The krone floats freely against the euro.
The krone has been replaced by the euro in Greenland and the Faroe Islands.
The krone is pegged to the pound sterling.
respuestas: The krone is pegged to the euro through ERM II.
preguntas.cita: the currency is pegged to the euro via the ERM II
preguntas.explicacion: Denmark keeps the krone, but it is linked to the euro through ERM II. It does not float freely, Greenland and the Faroe Islands also use the krone, and there is no link to the pound.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Luc Luycx, who designed the common sides of the coins, is a Belgian designer.
preguntas.explicacion: The text says that Luc Luycx designed the common sides, but it does not give his nationality. The only nationality mentioned is that of the banknote designer, the Austrian Robert Kalina.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 13 that means “advised against”.
preguntas.cita: This practice is discouraged by the commission
preguntas.explicacion: “Discouraged” means that the Commission advises against the practice without actually banning it.

preguntas.pregunta: What is shown on the back of euro banknotes?
preguntas.cita: while the back has bridges, symbolising links between states in the union and with the future
preguntas.explicacion: The reverse shows bridges, a symbol of the links between states. Windows and gateways are on the front; portraits are not mentioned and maps appear on the coins.

preguntas.enunciado: Say whether the statement is true, false or not stated in the text.
preguntas.pregunta: Since 2019, the €500 banknote is no longer legal tender.
preguntas.cita: both the first and the second series of euro banknotes, including the €500, remain legal tender throughout the euro area
preguntas.explicacion: The 500-euro note has not been issued since 2019, but it is still legal tender. The statement confuses the two and is false.

preguntas.pregunta: What share of the total value of euro banknotes does the ECB itself issue?
opciones: It depends on each country's GDP alone.
preguntas.cita: The ECB issues 8% of the total value of banknotes issued by the Eurosystem.
preguntas.explicacion: The ECB issues 8%; the remaining 92% is issued by the national central banks according to the capital key, which gives equal weight to population and GDP, not just GDP.

preguntas.enunciado: Answer in your own words (1–3 sentences).
preguntas.pregunta: How are euro transfers between EU countries treated, and what exception is mentioned?
respuestas: Transfers in euro within the EU, including card payments and ATM withdrawals in the eurozone, are treated as domestic transactions with domestic costs, even in member states outside the eurozone. The exception is paper-based payment orders such as cheques, which have not been standardised.
preguntas.cita: All intra-Union transfers in euro are treated as domestic transactions and bear the corresponding domestic transfer costs.
preguntas.explicacion: You should say that they are treated as domestic transactions at the same cost, and that cheques and paper orders are the exception because they are not standardised.

preguntas.enunciado: Find a word in paragraph 20 that means “openly disregarded”.
preguntas.cita: both of which were ultimately widely flouted after introduction
preguntas.explicacion: “To flout” is to break a rule openly or defiantly; here it refers to the deficit and debt limits.
